sentences.text: Eolambia is classified as a large hadrosauroid dinosaur.
This animal could measure up to 6 meters in length, with Gregory S. Paul estimating in 2016 that it reached a body length of 6 meters and a weight of 1 metric ton.
It possessed a crestless skull with a shape similar to that of Equijubus and Probactrosaurus.
Eolambia possessed highly opisthocoelous cervical vertebrae with strongly convex front ends and concave back ends, a trait shared with other styracosternans.
The scapular blade of Eolambia was nearly rectangular with straight sides meeting the blade end at almost a right angle, similar to Probactrosaurus.
The tips of Eolambia's premaxillae feature two tooth-like structures called denticles, a trait shared with Protohadros.
Fossils of Eolambia eggshells have been found at various localities alongside isolated teeth, showing reticular surface patterns and a thickness of 2 mm.
Evidence of scavenging includes severed Eolambia tibiae with tooth marks found in the Cifelli #2 quarry.
The number of maxilla teeth in Eolambia increased from 23 in juveniles to 33 in adults, a change well-documented because the species is known from both juvenile and adult specimens.
The only species of Eolambia is E. caroljonesa, named by James Kirkland in 1998.
In 1979, Galton and Jensen described a fragmentary femur (BYU 2000) from Arches National Park, Utah.
The Cifelli #2 Quarry is a specific locality associated with the river channel system where Eolambia fossils were found.
Eolambia is the most completely known iguanodont from the Cenomanian to Santonian stages.
Eolambia lived in humid floodplain forests near lakes and ate gymnosperms, ferns, and flowering plants.
Head found that Eolambia had broader, more asymmetrical teeth and that subadults possessed only two teeth per position, unlike hadrosaurids.
Eolambia possessed seven sacral vertebrae, whereas derived hadrosaurids have eight or more.
Kirkland suggested that basal hadrosaurids like Eolambia may have developed their antitrochanter later in life compared to derived hadrosaurids.

Juvenile Eolambia were preyed upon by large crocodylomorphs in the lake waters, while the abundance of juvenile fossils suggests that larger individuals were too big to be preyed upon by crocodilians.
Larger Eolambia were likely vulnerable to predation by the large neovenatorid theropod Siats.
Kirkland initially classified Eolambia as a member of the Hadrosauridae family based on a definition established in 1993.
Head concluded that Eolambia is a basal member of Hadrosauroidea outside the Hadrosauridae, closely related to Probactrosaurus.
Horner and colleagues identified Eolambia as a non-hadrosaurid hadrosauroid that was the sister group to Protohadros.
Kirkland debated whether Eolambia was a basal member of the Lambeosaurinae or their sister group, noting that recognizing it as a lambeosaurine would require redefining the subfamily.
Eolambia lived during the Cenomanian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
Eolambia lived between 121.4 and 93.9 million years ago during the Aptian and Cenomanian stages.

All known specimens of Eolambia have been found in Emery County, Utah, within the Mussentuchit Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation, on a poorly-drained floodplain near a system of large, perennial lakes.
Researchers caution that a deep dentary specimen might represent a distinct hadrosauroid rather than an unusual Eolambia.

Researchers Kirkland, Cifelli, and colleagues proposed that Eolambia arrived in North America from Asia during the Cenomanian, replacing native fauna, while other researchers contradict the Asian origin hypothesis by suggesting that the North American Protohadros is the closest relative of Eolambia.
